screens.title: Machine Language: Bits, Instructions, and the CPU
screens.narratorSegment: In this short module, we’ll treat machine language as a simple, precise code that the C P U reads without ambiguity. Every instruction the C P U executes is a 16-bit pattern of zeros and ones. Some patterns tell the C P U to load a value into a register; others tell the arithmetic logic unit to compute, store, or jump. Learning this language matters because it shows how high-level programs are grounded in hardware behavior, and it reveals why certain trade-offs—like reserving a leading bit to mark instruction type—exist. For example, the A-instruction begins with a zero and carries a 15-bit value to load into the A register. The C-instruction begins with three ones and then splits into an a bit, a six-bit comp field, three dest bits, and three jump bits to control computation, storage, and flow. A practical skill you’ll practice is translating assembly like D=M+1 into exactly sixteen bits, and back again. As you move through the lesson screens, notice how the fields map to hardware actions and how a small number of computations can be composed into many instruction encodings. Consider this question as you begin: how does a single leading bit let the C P U choose an entirely different interpretation of the remaining bits?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to move between human-readable assembly and machine code with confidence. First, you will understand how machine language relates to hardware: the C P U sees only bits, and instruction interpretation is driven by fixed bit positions. For a concrete example, you will read an A-instruction like at-sign forty-two and produce a 16-bit word with a leading zero and a fifteen-bit binary value. Second, you will be able to describe the C-instruction layout: the a bit chooses whether the ALU reads A or M, the comp bits define the ALU computation, the dest bits select where the result is stored, and the jump bits examine ALU flags. Third, you will translate assembly mnemonics such as D=M+1 into the exact sequence of bits and explain each field’s role. Fourth, you will explain how the C P U decodes those fields into hardware actions and why reserving a type bit is a deliberate design choice. Each skill ties a concrete example to the hardware behavior behind it.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Examples & Mnemonics
screens.narratorSegment: In this companion objectives screen, we reinforce the same four learning goals with examples and small visual mnemonics you can use while translating instructions. For understanding machine language and hardware, picture a sealed envelope of bits: the C P U opens the envelope and performs exactly what the pattern says. For instruction formats, recall the rule: zero leads an address; triple one leads a compute instruction. When translating assembly, practice by mapping each mnemonic to the comp, dest, and jump tables and writing the concatenated bits. For C P U decoding, imagine a small decoder circuit that checks the first three bits and routes the remaining bits to ALU controls, register write lines, or the program counter. Each card below gives a two-sentence skill description and a tiny mnemonic: envelope, flag, map, and decoder. Use these mental models to avoid common mistakes like misplacing the a bit or confusing dest bit order. That habit will make translations fast and accurate.

screens.title: Machine language as bits
screens.narratorSegment: Machine language is not a human language; it's a stream of bits that the C P U decodes and acts upon. At the hardware level there are no symbols or words, only voltage levels interpreted as zeros and ones. Each 16-bit instruction is a pattern where specific bit positions have fixed roles. The C P U fetches a 16-bit word from memory, then uses the leading bits to decide how to interpret the rest. For instance, when the first bit is zero the C P U treats the word as an A-instruction and loads the fifteen remaining bits into the A register. If the leading bits are three ones, the C P U interprets the word as a C-instruction and routes the remaining bits to ALU control logic, register write signals, and jump logic. A useful mental model is to think of an instruction as a labeled envelope: the label (leading bits) tells the C P U which internal mail slot to open. A common misconception is to imagine that every bit is free to mean anything; in reality, every position has a designed meaning, and misplacing a bit changes the instruction type or its behavior. Consider an example: the 16-bit word 0000000000000101 is not an arithmetic command; it is an A-instruction that sets A to five. Recognizing these distinct roles helps you reliably translate between assembly and binary.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An instruction is a 16-bit pattern; fixed bit positions determine whether the CPU treats it as an address load or as compute/store/jump control.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Machine language as bits
What an instruction is
A 16-bit word in memory. The CPU reads it and uses fixed bit positions to decide actions.
Type bit: first bit decides A vs C
Fields: value or control words follow the type bits
Hardware mapping: bits map directly to signals for registers, ALU, and PC
Common misconception
Bits are not arbitrary labels; moving a bit changes meaning. Treat each position as part of the instruction’s grammar.
Concrete examples
A-instruction example:
0000000000000101  // @5  -> load value 5 into A

C-instruction start:
111 a cccccc ddd jjj  // compute, store, jump
Key Takeaway

The instruction type bit(s) determine the decoding path; remaining bits have strictly assigned roles.

screens.title: A-instruction format and examples
screens.narratorSegment: The A-instruction is the simplest machine instruction in the Hack language. It is identified by a leading zero bit followed by fifteen bits that represent a nonnegative integer. When the C P U fetches such a pattern, it places the fifteen-bit value into the A register. This register can then be used as an address for R A M access or as an ALU input. A concrete example is the assembly directive at-sign forty-two. Translating it requires writing forty-two in binary and padding to fifteen bits: forty-two becomes 000000000101010, and with the leading zero the full instruction is 000000000101010. A common error students make is forgetting to pad to fifteen bits or accidentally setting the leading type bit to one, which would make the C P U treat the sequence as a C-instruction. Practically, the fifteen-bit limit means A-instructions can address memory and load constants within the range of zero to thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-seven. Think about this limit as a design trade-off: reserving a type bit simplifies decoding but reduces the immediate value range. Try translating @5, @0, and @32767 to see the padding and boundary behavior.

keyIdea.title: A-instruction
keyIdea.text: Encoded as 0 followed by a 15-bit value; used to load a value into the A register or specify an address.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › A-instruction format
Structure
Leading 0 then 15 bits encoding a numeric value. CPU loads the 15-bit value into A.
Use: load constant or set address for RAM access
Padding rule: always write the value in binary and pad with leading zeros to reach 15 bits.
Example translations
@5   -> 0000000000000101
@42  -> 000000000101010
@0   -> 0000000000000000
@32767 -> 0111111111111111
Errors to avoid
  • Forgetting to pad to 15 bits produces the wrong binary length.
  • Setting the first bit to one turns the word into a C-instruction.
  • Using a value > 32767 exceeds the A-instruction range.
Pro tip

Write the decimal value, convert to binary, then pad to 15 bits before adding the leading zero.

screens.title: C-instruction structure
screens.narratorSegment: A C-instruction is a compute instruction that combines ALU control, write destinations, and optional jump conditions. It always begins with three one bits, which tell the C P U to treat the remaining thirteen bits as control fields. The next bit, called the a bit, selects whether the ALU’s second operand is the A register or the memory location addressed by A. Following that are six comp bits that form the ALU control word; these bits select the exact arithmetic or logical operation the ALU performs. After comp come three dest bits that determine which of A, D, or M receives the ALU output. Finally the three jump bits indicate whether the program counter should be loaded from A depending on ALU flags. A common misunderstanding is to think comp encodes only simple operations; in reality the comp bits implement a small control language for the ALU using zeros and ones for input, inversion, function selection, and output negation. Concretely, the instruction field split looks like this: 111 a cccccc ddd jjj. Practice reading each field aloud as a role: a selects memory, comp computes, dest stores, and jump branches. That habit prevents mis-translation and makes debugging easier.

keyIdea.title: C-instruction anatomy
keyIdea.text: C-instruction splits control into a selector bit, a comp control word, destination bits, and jump bits; each maps to hardware signals.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › C-instruction structure
Bit fields and roles
111 — identify C-instruction
a — ALU y input selector (0: A, 1: M)
comp (6 bits) — ALU operation control word
dest (3 bits) — where ALU output is stored
jump (3 bits) — PC update condition based on ALU flags
Quick reference
Format:
111 a cccccc ddd jjj

Example fields:
a = 1  // use M as ALU input
comp = 110111  // M+1
dest = 010  // write to D
jump = 000  // no jump
Key Takeaway

C-instructions pack ALU control, destinations, and jump logic into a single 16-bit word so the CPU can compute and update state in one cycle.

screens.title: The comp field and ALU operations
screens.narratorSegment: The comp field is a six-bit control word that tells the ALU what to compute. Although there are sixty-four possible six-bit combinations, the Hack design delegates meaningful ALU functions to about eighteen combinations that correspond to conventional operations like zero, one, register D, register A or M, negations, increments, decrements, adds, subtracts, and bitwise AND/OR. Each comp code can be read as a compact recipe for disabling inputs, inverting, selecting add vs logical, and negating output. For example, the code for D plus A uses comp bits 000010, while M plus one is 110111 when the a bit is set. A practical way to work with comp is to memorize the common mappings and then fall back to table lookup for uncommon codes. A common misconception is to assume the comp field encodes high-level operators; instead it encodes low-level ALU micro-operations composed by signals named zx, nx, zy, ny, f, and no. When translating assembly like D=A you identify the comp code that produces A, then set dest bits appropriately and leave jump as zero. To check your understanding, try converting D-1 and A-1 to their comp codes and verify against the reference table. The comp field’s wide encoding space allows many combinations, but only a focused subset map to useful arithmetic or logical operations.

keyIdea.title: Comp field
keyIdea.text: Six bits configure the ALU; about eighteen combinations correspond to common, useful operations such as arithmetic and logical functions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Comp field & ALU
What comp does
Selects the ALU operation. Often these are small arithmetic and logical primitives used in programs.
Common comp codes
  • 101010 — 0
  • 111111 — 1
  • 001100 — D
  • 110000 — A (or M when a = 1)
  • 000010 — D + A
  • 010101 — D | A
Practice example
Translate operation: D = A - 1
Find comp code for A-1 -> 110010
Set a = 0 (uses A), comp = 110010, dest for D -> 010, jump -> 000
Full bits: 111 0 110010 010 000
Common mistake

Confusing A with M when a is wrong. Always set a correctly before choosing comp that references M.

screens.title: Dest field: where results go
screens.narratorSegment: The dest field in a C-instruction specifies which of the three destinations receives the ALU result: A register, D register, or M (the memory word addressed by A). It is encoded in three bits, each bit corresponding to one destination. For example, 010 writes the ALU output to D only; 101 writes to A and M simultaneously; 000 discards the result. This small set of combinations gives you flexible ways to store a result without extra instructions. When translating assembly like AMD equals D plus one, you set dest to 111 to update all three destinations at once. A common pitfall is misordering the bits — the bit positions correspond to A, D, M in the chapter’s table, and you must match that ordering when composing the binary word. Another practical note is that storing to M writes to R A M at the address currently in the A register, so an instruction that writes to M implicitly depends on a correct A value. Think about dest bits like mailboxes: each bit opens a mailbox that receives the ALU output. When you design sequences of instructions, choose dest combinations that minimize extra moves and keep the program compact.

keyIdea.title: Dest field
keyIdea.text: Three bits map to registers A, D, and memory M; combinations allow selective storage of ALU results.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Dest field
Dest bit meanings
Three bits select A, D, and M as destinations. Use combinations to write to multiple places in one instruction.
000 — null (discard ALU output)
001 — M
010 — D
111 — AMD (all destinations)
Example scenarios
If you want to copy D into memory at address A, use dest 001 and ensure A contains the target address. To increment a value and keep both A and D updated, use dest 101 or 111 depending on which registers you need.
Key Takeaway

Dest bits are simple but powerful for combining storage actions with computation in a single instruction.

screens.title: Jump field and ALU flags
screens.narratorSegment: The jump field controls program flow by telling the C P U whether to change the program counter based on the ALU’s output. The ALU sets two flags used by jump decisions: zero (zr) if the result equals zero, and negative (ng) if the result is negative. The three jump bits encode conditions like jump-if-greater-than-zero, jump-if-equal, jump-if-less-than-zero, and unconditional jump. For instance, JEQ uses the pattern where jump bits test the zero flag, while JGT requires not zero and not negative. When the jump condition is true, the C P U loads the address from the A register into the program counter so execution continues at that address. A misconception learners often have is thinking the jump bits cause computation; they do not. The ALU always computes first; the jump bits only inspect ALU flags and decide whether to change the control flow. For practice, imagine an ALU output of negative one: which jump conditions would trigger? JLT and JNE would fire in that case. Remember that jump bits are evaluated after the ALU produces flags, and they simply direct whether to set the PC from A.

keyIdea.title: Jump field
keyIdea.text: Three bits represent conditional tests (zr, ng) on ALU output; if the condition holds, PC is loaded from A.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Jump field & flags
ALU flags
The ALU sets zero (zr) and negative (ng) flags after computing. Jump bits evaluate these flags to choose control transfer.
  • 000 — null (no jump)
  • 001 — JGT (out > 0)
  • 010 — JEQ (out = 0)
  • 011 — JGE (out >= 0)
  • 100 — JLT (out < 0)
  • 111 — JMP (always)
Scenario check
Suppose ALU output is -1 (negative): JLT and JNE will be true. If output is 0, JEQ and JGE and JLE are true depending on bit patterns. Use A as the target address and ensure it contains the intended destination before the jump check.
Key Takeaway

Jump bits do not compute; they inspect ALU flags and conditionally update the program counter from A.

screens.title: Translate: D=M+1 → machine code
screens.narratorSegment: Let's translate a concrete C-instruction from assembly to machine code: D equals M plus one. First, identify that this is a C-instruction because it performs a computation and has a destination. The a bit should be one because the comp expression references M, not A, so ALU will read memory at address A for the second operand. Next find the comp bits for M plus one; the reference shows comp = 110111 for M+1. Then choose the dest bits: the destination is D only, which maps to 010. The jump field is empty, so it is 000. Now concatenate the fields: leading '111' to mark a C-instruction, then a = 1, comp = 110111, dest = 010, jump = 000. The final sixteen-bit machine code is 1111110111010000. A common mistake is to swap dest bit ordering or forget to set a to one, which would instead select A as the ALU input and produce a different comp meaning. To check your work, translate the bit string back to fields and verify each matches the original assembly components. This stepwise approach generalizes: determine instruction type, set a appropriately, look up comp, pick dest, set jump.

keyIdea.title: Translation pattern
keyIdea.text: Decide type, set a for M vs A, select comp, choose dest, set jump; then concatenate bits to form the 16-bit instruction.

content.html:

Step-by-step

screens.title: Reverse translation: binary to assembly
screens.narratorSegment: Translating binary back to assembly is a practiced reversal: parse the known field widths, interpret each, and render the assembly mnemonic. Start by checking the leading bit. If it is zero, you have an A-instruction and the remaining fifteen bits are a numeric value to write as at-sign value. If the first three bits are one-one-one, parse a single a bit, then six comp bits, three dest bits, and three jump bits. For a quick example, take the binary 1110110000010000. Leading 111 marks a C-instruction. The a bit is 0, comp bits are 110000 which correspond to A, dest bits are 010 meaning write to D, and jump bits are 000 meaning no jump. Combining those fields gives D=A as the assembly. For another example, 0000000000010100 is an A-instruction that holds decimal twenty because fifteen-bit binary 0000000000010100 equals twenty. A common error is mis-slicing the bit string; always use the fixed widths and double-check your comp table mapping. As you practice, translate the provided hands-on list both directions and verify each step by reconstructing the fields; this reinforces how every bit has a specific decoding role in the C P U.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Binary to Assembly
Parsing steps
  1. Check leading bits: 0 -> A-instruction, 111 -> C-instruction.
  2. If A-instruction: convert the remaining 15 bits to decimal for @value.
  3. If C-instruction: read a (1), comp (6), dest (3), jump (3).

Binary: 1110110000010000
Split: 111 0 110000 010 000
Interpret: a=0, comp=110000 -> A, dest=010 -> D, jump=000 -> null
Assembly: D=A

screens.title: CPU decoding and design trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: The C P U’s instruction decoder is simple because certain bit positions are reserved to identify instruction types and control signals. Reserving the first bit as zero for A-instructions and using three leading ones for C-instructions lets the C P U quickly choose between a load value path and a compute path. This simplicity comes with trade-offs. For example, because one bit is reserved for the instruction type, A-instructions hold only fifteen bits of data, limiting immediate values and address range to zero through thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-seven. That limit is acceptable in the Hack architecture because its memory size matches that range, but other architectures can choose different trade-offs between decoding complexity and immediate width. The C P U decodes by checking the leading bits, then routing the rest to simpler decoders: one converts bit fields to ALU control signals, another drives register write lines, and a third gates program-counter updates based on ALU flags. A common misunderstanding is to assume larger immediate fields are always better; instead, the design balances decoding cost, instruction density, and hardware simplicity. When you design or read instruction sets, ask which bits must be reserved to make decoding cheap and which bits should be flexible for expressiveness.

keyIdea.text: Reserved type bits make CPU decoding simple but limit immediate value range; this is a deliberate architecture trade-off.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › CPU decoding & trade-offs
Decoder principle
Check reserved bits to choose a decoding path. Simple checks reduce hardware complexity and latency.
Implementation blocks
  • Type detector (leading bits)
  • ALU control generator (comp and a)
  • Register write gating (dest)
  • PC update logic (jump + flags)
Design trade-off
Reserving bits keeps decoding cheap but reduces immediate width. Hack uses 15-bit immediates to match its memory size.
Key Takeaway

Simple decoders favor reserved type bits; the resulting immediate limits are an acceptable trade-off in small architectures like Hack.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: To summarize, machine language is a stream of binary patterns that the C P U decodes and executes directly. The Hack instruction set uses two 16-bit formats: A-instructions begin with zero and carry a fifteen-bit value for the A register, while C-instructions begin with three ones and split the remaining bits into an a selector, six comp bits for ALU control, three dest bits for storage, and three jump bits for control flow. The comp field implements a small set of useful ALU operations; the dest bits map outputs to A, D, and M; and the jump bits inspect ALU zero and negative flags to decide whether to load the program counter from A. A practical habit is to always identify the instruction type first, then parse or assemble the fields in order: a, comp, dest, jump. Remember that reserving type bits simplifies C P U decoding at the cost of immediate width. With these core ideas you can translate assembly to binary, reverse-engineer binary to assembly, and explain how the C P U turns bits into actions.

fullNarratorScript:
In this short module, we’ll treat machine language as a simple, precise code that the C P U reads without ambiguity. Every instruction the C P U executes is a 16-bit pattern of zeros and ones. Some patterns tell the C P U to load a value into a register; others tell the arithmetic logic unit to compute, store, or jump. Learning this language matters because it shows how high-level programs are grounded in hardware behavior, and it reveals why certain trade-offs—like reserving a leading bit to mark instruction type—exist. For example, the A-instruction begins with a zero and carries a 15-bit value to load into the A register. The C-instruction begins with three ones and then splits into an a bit, a six-bit comp field, three dest bits, and three jump bits to control computation, storage, and flow. A practical skill you’ll practice is translating assembly like D=M+1 into exactly sixteen bits, and back again. As you move through the lesson screens, notice how the fields map to hardware actions and how a small number of computations can be composed into many instruction encodings. Consider this question as you begin: how does a single leading bit let the C P U choose an entirely different interpretation of the remaining bits?

By the end of these screens you will be able to move between human-readable assembly and machine code with confidence. First, you will understand how machine language relates to hardware: the C P U sees only bits, and instruction interpretation is driven by fixed bit positions. For a concrete example, you will read an A-instruction like at-sign forty-two and produce a 16-bit word with a leading zero and a fifteen-bit binary value. Second, you will be able to describe the C-instruction layout: the a bit chooses whether the ALU reads A or M, the comp bits define the ALU computation, the dest bits select where the result is stored, and the jump bits examine ALU flags. Third, you will translate assembly mnemonics such as D=M+1 into the exact sequence of bits and explain each field’s role. Fourth, you will explain how the C P U decodes those fields into hardware actions and why reserving a type bit is a deliberate design choice. Each skill ties a concrete example to the hardware behavior behind it.

In this companion objectives screen, we reinforce the same four learning goals with examples and small visual mnemonics you can use while translating instructions. For understanding machine language and hardware, picture a sealed envelope of bits: the C P U opens the envelope and performs exactly what the pattern says. For instruction formats, recall the rule: zero leads an address; triple one leads a compute instruction. When translating assembly, practice by mapping each mnemonic to the comp, dest, and jump tables and writing the concatenated bits. For C P U decoding, imagine a small decoder circuit that checks the first three bits and routes the remaining bits to ALU controls, register write lines, or the program counter. Each card below gives a two-sentence skill description and a tiny mnemonic: envelope, flag, map, and decoder. Use these mental models to avoid common mistakes like misplacing the a bit or confusing dest bit order. That habit will make translations fast and accurate.

Machine language is not a human language; it's a stream of bits that the C P U decodes and acts upon. At the hardware level there are no symbols or words, only voltage levels interpreted as zeros and ones. Each 16-bit instruction is a pattern where specific bit positions have fixed roles. The C P U fetches a 16-bit word from memory, then uses the leading bits to decide how to interpret the rest. For instance, when the first bit is zero the C P U treats the word as an A-instruction and loads the fifteen remaining bits into the A register. If the leading bits are three ones, the C P U interprets the word as a C-instruction and routes the remaining bits to ALU control logic, register write signals, and jump logic. A useful mental model is to think of an instruction as a labeled envelope: the label (leading bits) tells the C P U which internal mail slot to open. A common misconception is to imagine that every bit is free to mean anything; in reality, every position has a designed meaning, and misplacing a bit changes the instruction type or its behavior. Consider an example: the 16-bit word 0000000000000101 is not an arithmetic command; it is an A-instruction that sets A to five. Recognizing these distinct roles helps you reliably translate between assembly and binary.

The A-instruction is the simplest machine instruction in the Hack language. It is identified by a leading zero bit followed by fifteen bits that represent a nonnegative integer. When the C P U fetches such a pattern, it places the fifteen-bit value into the A register. This register can then be used as an address for R A M access or as an ALU input. A concrete example is the assembly directive at-sign forty-two. Translating it requires writing forty-two in binary and padding to fifteen bits: forty-two becomes 000000000101010, and with the leading zero the full instruction is 000000000101010. A common error students make is forgetting to pad to fifteen bits or accidentally setting the leading type bit to one, which would make the C P U treat the sequence as a C-instruction. Practically, the fifteen-bit limit means A-instructions can address memory and load constants within the range of zero to thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-seven. Think about this limit as a design trade-off: reserving a type bit simplifies decoding but reduces the immediate value range. Try translating @5, @0, and @32767 to see the padding and boundary behavior.

A C-instruction is a compute instruction that combines ALU control, write destinations, and optional jump conditions. It always begins with three one bits, which tell the C P U to treat the remaining thirteen bits as control fields. The next bit, called the a bit, selects whether the ALU’s second operand is the A register or the memory location addressed by A. Following that are six comp bits that form the ALU control word; these bits select the exact arithmetic or logical operation the ALU performs. After comp come three dest bits that determine which of A, D, or M receives the ALU output. Finally the three jump bits indicate whether the program counter should be loaded from A depending on ALU flags. A common misunderstanding is to think comp encodes only simple operations; in reality the comp bits implement a small control language for the ALU using zeros and ones for input, inversion, function selection, and output negation. Concretely, the instruction field split looks like this: 111 a cccccc ddd jjj. Practice reading each field aloud as a role: a selects memory, comp computes, dest stores, and jump branches. That habit prevents mis-translation and makes debugging easier.

The comp field is a six-bit control word that tells the ALU what to compute. Although there are sixty-four possible six-bit combinations, the Hack design delegates meaningful ALU functions to about eighteen combinations that correspond to conventional operations like zero, one, register D, register A or M, negations, increments, decrements, adds, subtracts, and bitwise AND/OR. Each comp code can be read as a compact recipe for disabling inputs, inverting, selecting add vs logical, and negating output. For example, the code for D plus A uses comp bits 000010, while M plus one is 110111 when the a bit is set. A practical way to work with comp is to memorize the common mappings and then fall back to table lookup for uncommon codes. A common misconception is to assume the comp field encodes high-level operators; instead it encodes low-level ALU micro-operations composed by signals named zx, nx, zy, ny, f, and no. When translating assembly like D=A you identify the comp code that produces A, then set dest bits appropriately and leave jump as zero. To check your understanding, try converting D-1 and A-1 to their comp codes and verify against the reference table. The comp field’s wide encoding space allows many combinations, but only a focused subset map to useful arithmetic or logical operations.

The dest field in a C-instruction specifies which of the three destinations receives the ALU result: A register, D register, or M (the memory word addressed by A). It is encoded in three bits, each bit corresponding to one destination. For example, 010 writes the ALU output to D only; 101 writes to A and M simultaneously; 000 discards the result. This small set of combinations gives you flexible ways to store a result without extra instructions. When translating assembly like AMD equals D plus one, you set dest to 111 to update all three destinations at once. A common pitfall is misordering the bits — the bit positions correspond to A, D, M in the chapter’s table, and you must match that ordering when composing the binary word. Another practical note is that storing to M writes to R A M at the address currently in the A register, so an instruction that writes to M implicitly depends on a correct A value. Think about dest bits like mailboxes: each bit opens a mailbox that receives the ALU output. When you design sequences of instructions, choose dest combinations that minimize extra moves and keep the program compact.

The jump field controls program flow by telling the C P U whether to change the program counter based on the ALU’s output. The ALU sets two flags used by jump decisions: zero (zr) if the result equals zero, and negative (ng) if the result is negative. The three jump bits encode conditions like jump-if-greater-than-zero, jump-if-equal, jump-if-less-than-zero, and unconditional jump. For instance, JEQ uses the pattern where jump bits test the zero flag, while JGT requires not zero and not negative. When the jump condition is true, the C P U loads the address from the A register into the program counter so execution continues at that address. A misconception learners often have is thinking the jump bits cause computation; they do not. The ALU always computes first; the jump bits only inspect ALU flags and decide whether to change the control flow. For practice, imagine an ALU output of negative one: which jump conditions would trigger? JLT and JNE would fire in that case. Remember that jump bits are evaluated after the ALU produces flags, and they simply direct whether to set the PC from A.

Let's translate a concrete C-instruction from assembly to machine code: D equals M plus one. First, identify that this is a C-instruction because it performs a computation and has a destination. The a bit should be one because the comp expression references M, not A, so ALU will read memory at address A for the second operand. Next find the comp bits for M plus one; the reference shows comp = 110111 for M+1. Then choose the dest bits: the destination is D only, which maps to 010. The jump field is empty, so it is 000. Now concatenate the fields: leading '111' to mark a C-instruction, then a = 1, comp = 110111, dest = 010, jump = 000. The final sixteen-bit machine code is 1111110111010000. A common mistake is to swap dest bit ordering or forget to set a to one, which would instead select A as the ALU input and produce a different comp meaning. To check your work, translate the bit string back to fields and verify each matches the original assembly components. This stepwise approach generalizes: determine instruction type, set a appropriately, look up comp, pick dest, set jump.
